newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Croats alleges mini-state disbanded.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Croats alleges mini-state disbanded.

text.p: A Croat leader said on Thursday a separate mini-state in Bosnia had been officially disbanded -- a step the Croats had promised but failed to take for two years.

The Croat member of Bosnia's joint presidency, Kresimir Zubak, sent an open letter to U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum and the international High Representative to Bosnia, Carl Bildt, saying the ministries of the self-declared state had stopped functioning.

A Bosnian Croat news agency reported that Zubak's letter said the self-styled state was dismantled now that Moslem and Croat officials agreed on regulations over "the allocation of revenues" in the Moslem-Croat federation.

"(The Bosnian Croat leadership) will make further efforts to continue the positive trend of strengthening mutual trust and of setting up the functioning federal authorities," the Bosnian branch of the Croatian Democratic Union said.

Bosnian Croats have been repeatedly criticised by the international community for failing to disband the "Herceg- Bosna" administration which worked to create a separate state linked to neighbouring Croatia.
A spokesman for the High Representative said the letter was being taken at "face value" and would help strengthen Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation.
"We believe it's a positive step towards the total integration of the Croat element within the federation," spokesman Duncan Bullivant told Reuters.
Zubak met the deputy to the High Representative, Michael Steiner, on Thursday and told him the move was "unilateral", he said.
Similar claims dating back to 1994 have proved false.

Political analysts said Croat authorities continue to resist sharing power or giving up authority over Croat-held areas seized during the war, undermining efforts at building a post- war government in Bosnia.
The announcement coincided with an alarming rise in ethnic expulsions in Croat-held western Mostar.
Human rights workers and other Western officials have condemned Bosnian Croat authorities for failing to halt expulsions of Moslems and Serbs from western Mostar over the past two months.
The letter also came a day after the troubled Moslem-Croat federation approved a new peacetime cabinet.

The 15-member cabinet, headed by a Moslem prime minister, is supposed to take over many of the duties of the country's wartime government in Sarajevo. The outgoing cabinet held its last session this week.
After post-war elections held in September, most government authority passes to Bosnia's federation and Serb republic.
A weak central government, comprised of a collective presidency and a council of ministers, will oversee foreign trade, foreign affairs and communications ministries.
